scenario: WIBTA for faking a note to my child from their biological Father? | I'm about to become a single mother by choice. My sperm bank provides a lot of information about the donor. A physical description, medical history, professional background, a list of hobbies/interests, a childhood picture of the donor etc. Some donors are open to being contacted when the child is an adult. I wanted to find a donor open to this but I was not able to. I chose my donor because he matched all of the other requirements relating to health and was from the same ethnic background as me. That sounds bad, but I feel a strong connection to my home country even though I no longer live there, and it was important to me that my child be the same ethnicity. No other donors matched ethnic background AND my other requirements. Men of my ethnicity don't commonly donate. This wasn't a decision I took lightly. I considered many profiles. I spent weeks deciding. None of the open donors felt right. I don't feel positive about the closed donation. I'd feel unsatisfied never knowing or being able to have a conversation with a biological half of me but I've talked it through with a therapist and come to accept that my family can be enough for my child. I'm taking steps to give my child an idea of the biological half they are missing by making an identity box. I included all of the information I have on the donor in the box and my child will grow up understanding their background and the reasons they don't have a father. One of the reasons I made my peace with the closed donation is that the bank promised a letter from the donor to the child. I thought at least a letter could give an older child or teenager some closure if they were curious about their biological Father. I received the letter last week. It really isn't a letter. It's clear that the donor was asked to write something while in the office for medicals or something and wrote on a scrap of paper in a hurry. It's a photocopy of the paper and the note is three lines in total. Without quoting verbatim it says: "This is the strangest thing I've done but it's cool I get to help someone have kids! Good luck in life. I hope it works out for you." It feels anti-climatic to me so I can only imagine how it will feel to my child. I was talking to a friend about it this weekend and I mentioned that I was thinking of typing up something 'from' the donor that was a little more encouraging or at least a little longer. I wouldn't change the essence of the note but I would expand on it so it didn't feel so half-assed. I feel terrible for my child. I know I'll provide all the love and stability in the world but there will come a time when they will wonder. I'm not sure what to do, but my friend advised me that I'm overly emotional at the moment due to hormones and it wouldn't be fair to fake the note even if my child will never find out. I think she's probably right but I'm tempted to give my child more than they've been offered here. WIBTA?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently while keeping the festive spirit alive: ### **1. Clean & Prep the House (Most Important First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, dining area, entrance). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and storage spaces. - **Launder bedding, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least dust them). - **Wash windows/mirrors** for a bright, welcoming look. - *Why?* A clean home feels sacred and ready for guests—it’s the foundation for decorations. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decorative Lights)** - **Place diyas** in key areas: - **Entrance** (mandatory for Diwali—use a small table or wall-mounted holder). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Dining area** (if space allows). - **Balcony/porch** (if you have one). - **Use LED string lights** for a modern touch (safe and energy-efficient). - **Marigold garlands** (traditional) or **fairy lights** (for a soft glow). - *Tip:* If short on time, focus on the **entrance and living room** first—they make the biggest impact. ### **3. Quick Decor Updates (Minimal Effort, Big Impact)** - **Hang rangoli** (even a simple design at the entrance or near diyas). - **Place small decorative items**: - **Diwali-themed candles** (scented ones add ambiance). - **Mini statues** (Ganesha, Lakshmi, or lotus motifs). - **Fresh flowers** (marigolds or jasmine for a natural touch). - **Swap out throw pillows/blankets** for festive colors (gold, red, or orange). ### **4. Final Touches (Last-Minute)** - **Set up a small altar** (if you observe puja) with diyas, flowers, and incense. - **Arrange snacks/drinks** in a pretty tray (for guests). - **Test all lights** (diyas, bulbs, etc.) to avoid last-minute issues. - **Spritz air fresheners** (sandalwood or rose-scented) for a fresh feel. ### **5. Day Before Diwali (Quick Checklist)** - **Replenish diyas** (if using oil-based ones). - **Charge phone/laptop** (for photos/videos). - **Set out guest seating** (if hosting). - **Prepare a welcome note** (on the door or entrance). --- ### **Time-Saving Tips:** ✅ **DIY shortcuts**: - Use **glow sticks** (cheap and safe) as temporary diyas. - **Paint rocks** with gold paint for instant decor. - **Buy pre-made rangoli stencils** or use chalk for quick designs. ✅ **Delegate**: - Ask a family member to handle **lighting** while you focus on **cleaning**. - If you have kids, let them help with **hanging garlands or placing small diyas**. ✅ **Skip perfection**: - A few well-placed diyas + a clean entrance look **far more festive** than half-decorated rooms. --- ### **Sample Timeline (If You’re Short on Time):** - **Day 1 (Today)**: Clean + place diyas in entrance/living room. - **Day 2**: Add rangoli, garlands, and small decor items. - **Day 3 (Before Diwali)**: Final touches (lights, snacks, altar). --- **Most important priority?** **Cleanliness + entrance diyas**—they set the tone for guests. The rest can be layered in gradually. Wishing you a joyful Diwali! 🪔✨

I think she's probably right but I'm tempted to give my child more than they've been offered here. WIBTA?

It’s short, but it’s his way of being part of your story. I know it might not feel like enough, and that’s okay. Your family and your own journey are what matter most."* - This **validates your child’s feelings** without lying. #### **6. Even if your child never finds out, the **potential for confusion or distrust** is too high. 2. **Your child’s emotional resilience is better served by honesty**. They’ll handle the donor’s minimal note better if they know it’s real—and they’ll handle the absence of a father figure better if they know they’re loved unconditionally by you. 3. **This isn’t about "giving your child more"—it’s about controlling their narrative**. Your child’s identity is theirs to explore, not yours to shape. 4. **There are better ways to honor the donor’s role** (e.g., the alternatives above) without crossing into lying. --- ### **What You Can Do Instead:** - **Accept the donor’s note as-is** and **frame it as part of their unique story**. You might say: *"This is what your donor wrote when you were created. It’s not much, but it’s his way of being here for you. These are **far more meaningful** than a polished note. - **Prepare for questions**. If your child asks about the donor later, you can say: *"I know it feels like there’s a piece missing, but your family is your home.
